comparison: Both support Heron's core design philosophy and dual-level implementation (C1, C2, C7, C11, C73). OpenEval provides detailed architectural analysis while peer review confirms the software is 'valuable' with 'solid design' and 'functionally reliable.' Peer review also includes distributed computing claims (C3, C8, C23, C115) and language flexibility (C12-C14, C116-C117) that OpenEval addresses separately.

Both support multi-machine distributed capabilities. OpenEval focuses on technical implementation (C3, C8, C23, C24, C38, C56, C115) with Figure 4 evidence. Peer review confirms utility across heterogeneous environments without detailed technical analysis. Partial overlap on distributed computing claims.

Both support Python rationale and multi-language integration (C12-C14, C25-C26, C92, C116-C117). OpenEval provides detailed technical justification with Unity/C# example. Peer review acknowledges these capabilities as part of overall 'solid design' assessment.

Both support language and platform claims. OpenEval addresses Python choice and multi-language capability (C25, C26, C92). Peer review confirms platform compatibility (C24) and acknowledges lightweight, open-source nature without raising concerns about language claims.

Both support Node architecture claims (C27-C30). OpenEval provides detailed architectural analysis with Figure 1B reference. Peer review confirms 'solid design' and 'functionally reliable' without specific architectural concerns. Peer review also covers broader process architecture (C31-C38) that OpenEval addresses separately.

Both support process architecture and actor-based model (C31, C33-C37). OpenEval provides detailed technical analysis with Figure 2 and process count formula. Peer review acknowledges actor-based implementation as part of 'solid design' assessment.

Both support code architecture and technical requirements (C39-C42, C102-C111). OpenEval provides comprehensive documentation analysis of folder structure and message formats. Peer review confirms software is 'well documented' with 'special attention to documenting usage' without specific technical concerns.

Both support self-documentation benefit (C21, C32, C72, C122). OpenEval notes this is 'somewhat subjective' depending on user experience. Peer review explicitly identifies knowledge graph self-documentation as a key strength for 'readability and reproducibility,' providing stronger endorsement.

Both support extensibility features and development tools (C43-C44, C47-C49, C112-C114). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of repository structure and templates. Peer review confirms software is 'well documented' as part of overall assessment.

Both support repository structure and community design (C49, C113-C114). OpenEval focuses on technical extensibility features. Peer review emphasizes documentation quality and potential for 'wide adoption in many other experimental settings.'

Both strongly support the Probabilistic Reversal Learning example (C50, C70-C71, C120). OpenEval provides detailed walkthrough with Figure 3 reference. Peer review explicitly highlights knowledge graph self-documentation as enhancing 'readability and reproducibility.'

Both strongly support Fetching experiment demonstrating heterogeneous computing (C51-C56). OpenEval provides detailed technical analysis of hardware constraints and multi-environment setup. Peer review identifies distributed execution across different OS/hardware as a 'key strength' addressing 'commonly seen issue nowadays.'

Both support Unity integration and performance claims (C57-C62, C86). OpenEval provides detailed technical descriptions and CPU measurements. Peer review acknowledges 'sophisticated experimental setups' demonstrating functional reliability without questioning performance data.

Perfect claim overlap (C63-C65, C82-C85). Both support synchronization capabilities and low frame loss demonstration. OpenEval provides detailed technical analysis with Figure 5C reference. Peer review implicitly accepts through 'functionally reliable' assessment without raising concerns.

Both support on-the-fly parameter updates (C66). OpenEval provides technical description with state machine implementation. Peer review explicitly lists GUI control panel for parameter updates as a key strength, providing direct endorsement.

OpenEval rates learning curve claims (C4, C74, C118) as UNCERTAIN due to lack of empirical validation. Peer review implicitly supports these claims by noting Python code is 'more friendly to those who do not have a strong programming background' without questioning the assertions.

OpenEval questions user requirement claims (C74) as lacking empirical validation. Peer review supports accessibility through documentation quality and states software 'can be widely adopted,' suggesting acceptance of ease-of-use claims.

Perfect claim overlap (C5, C6, C9, C10). Both support background context and problem framing. OpenEval notes C5's 'practically impossible' is 'somewhat hyperbolic.' Peer review accepts motivation by stating software 'addresses a growing need' without questioning problem framing.

Perfect claim overlap (C15-C20). Both support related work descriptions and positioning. OpenEval confirms proper citations and accurate framework descriptions. Peer review implicitly accepts comparison by acknowledging Heron 'answers the need of experimentalists' without questioning positioning.

Both support GUI capabilities (C45-C46). OpenEval confirms network configuration and many-to-many connectivity as straightforward technical capabilities. Peer review notes 'clean and easy-to-use GUI' as part of overall positive assessment.

Both support animal details and experimental conditions (C67-C71, C123-C125). OpenEval confirms standard reporting requirements are met. Peer review implicitly accepts through overall approval without raising ethical or methodological concerns.

Both support methodological details (C67, C124-C125). OpenEval confirms ethical approval and reporting standards. Peer review implicitly accepts these details as part of 'well documented' software package per reviewer's statement.

Both support open-source nature and community vision (C75-C77, C119). OpenEval analyzes MIT license and repository rationale as design philosophy statements. Peer review emphasizes documentation quality and potential for wide adoption, supporting community-oriented goals.

Both support performance trade-offs and optimization features (C79-C81). OpenEval acknowledges CPU overhead as design trade-off with core pinning demonstration. Peer review accepts through 'functionally reliable' assessment without questioning performance claims.

Both support flexibility philosophy (C89-C91). OpenEval notes C89's 'very few limitations' claim is 'somewhat overstated' given specific constraints. Peer review supports flexibility by noting users supply Python code 'more friendly to those without strong programming background.'

Both support example rationale (C120-C122). OpenEval finds reasoning for not sharing files 'practical and reasonable' though ease of recreation depends on user experience. Peer review implicitly accepts through acknowledgment that examples demonstrate utility effectively.

Both support methodological decisions (C121-C122). OpenEval finds hardware dependency reasoning practical. Peer review implicitly accepts by stating 'authors have addressed concerns from initial review,' suggesting methodological choices are satisfactory.
